title: Tactical decision-making following filanesia-based ecological dynamics in youth football through a multisite cluster-randomized trial
venue: Journal of Coaching and Sports Science
abstract: Background: National playing philosophies can guide youth development, but whether a culturally situated framework offers lasting benefits beyond generic game-based practice remains unclear. Aims: This study compared Filanesia-based ecological dynamics (Filanesia-ED), generic ecological dynamics (Generic-ED), and conventional coaching for retained tactical decision-making, multidomain tactical adaptation, and pressure-stratified decision accuracy. Methods: A multisite three-arm cluster-randomized trial involved 144 players nested in 12 youth football teams in Lampung and North Sumatra, Indonesia. Teams completed 16 sessions over eight weeks, with assessment at pretest, posttest, and four-week retention. Analyses included longitudinal tactical outcomes, 9,806 match-decision events, 192 fidelity observations, and 1,152 small-sided-game GPS records. Player outcomes were analyzed longitudinally, and decision events were examined using generalized estimating equations. Findings were interpreted in the context of 12 randomized teams. Result: The longitudinal model showed a condition-by-time interaction, Wald χ²(4) = 363.83, p < .001. At posttest, the adjusted Filanesia-ED advantage was 12.59 points versus conventional coaching (95% CI [8.51, 16.67]) and 6.32 points versus Generic-ED (95% CI [2.25, 10.39]); corresponding retention differences were 11.33 and 6.75 points. In the event-level analysis, Filanesia-ED had higher odds of a correct decision under high opponent pressure than conventional coaching, OR = 1.74, 95% CI [1.33, 2.27], p < .001. Conclusion: Filanesia-ED was associated with higher posttest and retained tactical decision-making scores than either comparison. objective: Comparar si una versión culturalmente adaptada de dinámica ecológica (Filanesia-ED) aporta más toma de decisiones táctica retenida que una dinámica ecológica genérica o el entrenamiento convencional.
design: Ensayo aleatorizado por clústeres, multicéntrico, de tres brazos; 16 sesiones en 8 semanas con pretest, postest y retención a 4 semanas.
population: 144 jugadores de 12 equipos de fútbol base en Lampung y Sumatra Norte (Indonesia); 9.806 eventos de decisión, 192 observaciones de fidelidad y 1.152 registros GPS de juegos reducidos.
method: Se compararon los tres enfoques en puntuaciones tácticas longitudinales y en la corrección de decisiones en partido (ecuaciones de estimación generalizadas), estratificando por presión del rival.
results: Interacción condición×tiempo significativa (Wald χ²(4)=363,83; p<0,001). En el postest, Filanesia-ED superó al entrenamiento convencional en 12,59 puntos (IC95% 8,51–16,67) y a Generic-ED en 6,32; en retención, 11,33 y 6,75 puntos. Con alta presión rival, la probabilidad de decidir bien fue mayor que con el convencional (OR=1,74; IC95% 1,33–2,27).
conclusions: El enfoque Filanesia-ED se asoció a mejores decisiones tácticas, también retenidas, que las dos alternativas; los resultados multidominio son exploratorios.
limitations: Solo 12 clústeres, seguimiento corto y resultados multidominio exploratorios; hace falta replicar.
why: Es un ensayo aleatorizado de dinámica ecológica en fútbol base con retención, algo poco frecuente en tu línea; sugiere que adaptar el diseño de tareas al contexto cultural suma sobre el enfoque genérico.

title: Blocked vs. randomized practice shapes coordination across adaptation, retention, and transfer following perturbation-based balance training in young adults
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Perturbation-based balance training (PBT) improves reactive balance control, but it remains unclear whether increased practice variability, particularly the contextual interference effect (CIE), enhances retention and transfer. This study investigated whether blocked vs. randomized PBT schedules differently influence adaptation, retention, transfer, and coordination patterns. Thirty-two healthy young adults completed a single-session PBT with repeated trip perturbations under either a blocked or randomized schedule. Retention and intra-task transfer were evaluated using trained and untrained trip perturbations, and inter-task transfer was tested with a simulated forward fall. Dynamic stability performance was assessed using the margin of stability (MoS), and whole-body kinematic synergies (kSYNs) were extracted via principal component analysis to investigate coordinative changes. No significant improvements in MoS were observed during practice, and contrary to expectations derived from the CIE, randomized practice did not show superior retention, or transfer compared to blocked practice at the performance level. kSYNs revealed training-related adaptations and group differences, including changes in knee flexion contribution and stepping coordination. However, limited shared kSYNs between perturbed walking and simulated forward falls indicate strong task specificity. Together, these findings suggest that practice schedule influenced coordination patterns but did not translate into superior stability outcomes in young adults following single-session PBT.

title: "Beyond practice hours"- A systematic review of elite football development pathways.
venue: Frontiers in sports and active living
abstract: This systematic review synthesised research on the developmental activities of elite male football players and evaluated what existing evidence reveals about variation in developmental pathways across populations and contexts. Guided by the Developmental Model of Sport Participation, a framework synthesis was employed to integrate predominantly quantitative data within a qualitative, context-sensitive approach. Eighteen peer-reviewed studies were included following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, examining engagement in domain-specific activities (structured training, competition and informal play) and non-domain-specific activities (other sports). Early exposure to football was consistent across the reviewed studies, with differentiation towards elite performance emerging during adolescence through increased structured, coach-led practice. Evidence supporting early diversification was inconsistent, while engagement in informal play varied considerably across populations. Although developmental activity patterns differed between populations, the primary studies rarely measured the socio-cultural, institutional or environmental conditions potentially associated with these differences. The review extends existing knowledge by distinguishing between evidence describing what elite players did during development and evidence explaining why particular developmental pathways emerged. The findings suggest that expertise development may reflect a dynamic interaction between structured training and socio-cultural environments, supporting a context-dependent understanding of football expertise. Future research should combine developmental activity histories with direct measurements of contextual factors to better explain how different pathways to elite football emerge. PROSPERO identifier

title: Impact of Brainstorming-Driven Bounded Spaces Method on Developing Certain Creative Kinesthetic Abilities in Intermediate School Students
venue: International Journal of Experimental Sports Science Research
abstract: Backgroud: Traditional physical education instruction in soccer frequently relies on decontextualized command drills that detach motor execution from perceptual problem-solving. This study investigates the pedagogical impact of an 8-unit brainstorming-driven small-sided games curriculum (bounded spaces method) on developing fundamental soccer skills (ball control, slalom dribbling, and target shooting accuracy) and motor decision-making among male intermediate school students. Methods: A quasi-experimental non-equivalent control group pre-test/post-test design was conducted with 30 male second-intermediate students (aged 13–14 years) at Al-Haritha High School for Outstanding Students in Basra, Iraq, during the 2023–2024 academic year. Participants were assigned to an experimental group (n = 15, instructed via brainstorming-driven small-sided games across 4 weeks, 2 sessions/week, 45 min/session) or a control group (n = 15, instructed via conventional direct command drills). Skill batteries demonstrated high test-retest reliability (r = 0.86–0.89). Data were evaluated using paired and independent t-tests (df = 14 and df = 28), 95% confidence intervals, and effect size calculations (Cohen's d and Hedges' g). Results: While pre-test baseline measures confirmed group equivalence (p > 0.80), post-test evaluations demonstrated statistically significant superiority for the experimental group across all technical measures: ball control (mean = 8.933 vs. 7.733 points, t = 2.369, p = 0.025, Cohen's d = 0.866, 95% CI [0.163, 2.237]), dribbling agility time (mean = 12.951 s vs. 14.289 s, t = 3.229, p = 0.003, Cohen's d = -1.180, 95% CI [-2.187, -0.489]), and shooting accuracy (mean = 9.066 vs. 7.866 points, t = 2.662, p = 0.013, Cohen's d = 0.973, 95% CI [0.277, 2.123]). title: The E³P model: perception of external events and exposures in sport and exercise
venue: International Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology
abstract: Research on perception, attention, and appraisal in sport and exercise is extensive and influential. Building on this foundation, the Integrative External Events and Exposures Perception (E³P) model is introduced as a scaffold that connects established insights and clarifies implications for research and practice. The model conceptualises perception broadly as the conversion of external events into internal information. It frames the process in three components: (a) input, encompassing sensory energies and exogenous substances that, once taken up, generate perceivable internal signals; (b) attention allocation, conceived as a depth valve that routes processing along a shallow–to–deep continuum, alongside breadth, stability, and flexibility; and (c) a four-layer sequence of meaning-making—pre-attentive perception, stimulus-driven noticing, contextual interpretation, and evaluative appraisal—that operates cumulatively and concurrently. The model outlines multiple feed-forward and feedback loops within a perception–action cycle, together with continuous interactions with proprioception, internally directed attention, and self-regulation. The model components are mapped onto five applied approaches – game-based task design, technology-mediated simulations, sensory and physiological optimisation, cognitive–attentional training, and long-term personal development – to support athlete learning and development, elite performance, and inclusive practice across diverse participants. title: “Expertise guides where attention lies”: exploring climbers’ attentional focus during route preview using eye-tracking and verbal reports
venue: International Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology
abstract: Route preview, the visual inspection of climbing movements prior to motor execution, has attracted scientific interest over the past decades. From a sport psychology perspective, elucidating factors underlying differences in attentional focus during route preview appears promising for advancing understanding of how expertise shapes attentional processes in climbing and other relatively closed sporting contexts. This study examined attentional focus during route preview across climbers of varying skill levels by analysing gaze behaviour using portable eye-tracking. Twenty-five intermediate, advanced, and elite climbers previewed and attempted an Olympic boulder problem. Data collection included gaze behaviour during route preview alongside concurrent think-aloud and retrospective verbal reports, as well as climbing performance metrics. Besides lower climbing performance, intermediate climbers showed longer preview and total absolute fixation durations at holds than advanced and elite climbers. Despite similar overall relative fixations, the spatial distribution of these fixations differed between the groups; advanced and elite climbers displayed a more homogeneous pattern with lower variability, allocating a greater proportion of fixations to the middle and final sections of the boulder, whereas intermediate climbers focused more on the starting section. Verbal reports similarly revealed skill-level differences in attentional distribution and factors shaping attentional focus toward task-relevant holds. Findings suggest that attentional focus during route preview reflects an interplay among cognitive processing of movement demands, task difficulty relative to skill level, and perceived task-relevant priorities. title: Tactical behaviour in elite U-12 boys’ tennis: an observational mixed methods case study of the Open Super 12 Auray tournament
abstract: Evidence on tactical behaviour in elite U-12 tennis remains limited, particularly regarding how the serve interacts with rally development and point outcome. This observational mixed methods case study used a quantitatively driven qual → QUAN → qual analytical sequence to characterise the tactical profile of elite international U-12 boys competing at the 2023 Open Super 12 Auray tournament. Spontaneous match behaviours were systematically observed, transformed into coded categorical data using the OBSTENNIS-JUNIOR-S23 observational instrument, analysed quantitatively, and subsequently interpreted within their competitive and developmental context. A total of 557 points from seven matches involving eight players were analysed. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, Cramér’s V, adjusted standardised residuals, and conditional winning probabilities were calculated. Point outcome was relatively balanced between server (46.7%) and receiver (53.3%). After excluding double faults, the server won 53.7% of first-serve points and 43.3% of second-serve points. Body serves predominated overall (59.4%) and were especially frequent on second serves (91.0%). Short rallies accounted for 53.1% of points, although rally length was not associated with point outcome. Unforced errors were the main route to point resolution. The integrated observational mixed methods approach enabled the construction of a contextualised tactical profile of elite U-12 boys’ tennis. These findings indicate that, in this competitive case, the serve did not provide a clear overall tactical advantage and support training approaches that combine serve-placement variability, serve–return–third-shot sequences, rally consistency, and error management.

title: Braid Complexity and Peloton Phase Dynamics
abstract: Section: Preprints Categories: Sport Science, Statistics, Metascience Keywords: peloton, cycling, braid complexity, phase transitions, collective behavior, Netlogo simulations A peloton is a complex, self-organizing system whose collective behavior is driven largely by energetic coupling, described by the peloton convergence ratio (PCR) and positional ordering, described here as braid complexity (C x *). We formalize peloton phase states by combining PCR with C x *, yielding a coupled energetic-positional index, C x P*. Through time-series segmentation of empirical mass-start data and NetLogo simulations, we develop a phase-space framework comprising compact, stretched, and decoupled states and associated subphases. The inclusion of directional microphases—acceleration (Da) and deceleration (Dd)—reveals a hysteresis-like asymmetry within high-PCR/low-C x * states, indicating a stretched-fatigued (Sf) state as a deceleration-driven counterpart to the standard stretched (S) phase. A multivariate approach provides a useful framework for characterizing self-organized transitions in pelotons and may help inform future study of other self-propelled biological collectives by linking individual physiological limits with group-level structural dynamics.

title: Reconfiguring coaching expertise in datafied sport: From knowledge possession to knowledge orchestration
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: Although data and digital analytics are increasingly used in sport, their implications for coaching decision-making and expertise remain insufficiently understood. This study examined how data and digital analytics were incorporated into coaching judgement and decision-making and what these processes meant for the reconfiguration of coaching expertise. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with four coaches, three data and analytics specialists, and three athletes with experience in data-informed coaching in elite and professional sport. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that data did not replace experiential judgement but extended what could be perceived and traced over time, while providing additional grounds on which existing assessments could be reviewed. However, greater access to information did not make coaching decisions self-evident or necessarily more objective. Participants interpreted data's meaning and limitations contextually and selectively weighted diverse forms of evidence. Interpretive work and epistemic authority were distributed among coaches, analysts, and athletes, rendering decision-making more negotiated, whereas authority and accountability for final decisions remained largely with coaches. Taken together, the findings indicated that coaching expertise was being reconfigured around the capacity to orchestrate distributed knowledge, explain, justify, and revise professional judgements, and remain accountable for decisions made under uncertainty. These findings suggest that coach education should extend beyond technical data literacy to develop capacities for contextual interpretation, knowledge orchestration, and accountable professional judgement.

title: Goalkeeper profiles in the English women's super league: Seasonal trends, team-quality contexts, and implications for coaching practice
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: Goalkeeper roles in football are increasingly multidimensional, yet goalkeeper-specific evidence in elite women's football remains limited. This study examined goalkeeper match behaviours in the English Women's Super League across seven available seasons, focusing on seasonal trends and team-quality differences. Hudl StatsBomb event data covered 853 matches, 17 teams, and 71 goalkeepers. Goalkeeper actions were grouped into attacking and defensive domains, standardised using per-match and proportional metrics, and analysed using descriptive statistics, multiple factor analysis, Ward.D2 hierarchical clustering, and regression models appropriate to count and cluster-membership outcomes. Attacking actions accounted for 80.92% of included goalkeeper actions. Cluster analysis identified two dominant profiles, Possession organiser and Goal defender, alongside two rare, event-defined situational subprofiles, Sweeper and Active intervener. The possession organiser profile was dominant, representing 77.7% of team-match observations, while the goal defender profile represented 15.4%. Across seasons, goalkeeper involvement showed a shift towards greater possession involvement, with increases in passing, carrying, ball receipts, and keeper-sweeper actions. Team quality was associated with differences in goalkeeper profiles: Top 4 teams showed greater possession involvement and more possession organiser profiles, whereas Low-ranking teams showed greater defensive workload and more goal defender profiles. These findings support a layered approach to goalkeeper profiling, in which broad possession- and defence-oriented involvement is interpreted alongside rare but tactically meaningful situational actions.

title: Playing up the ladder: GPS-derived match physical outputs of youth soccer players promoted to a higher age category
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: This study examined the GPS-derived match physical outputs of youth soccer players promoted to compete in a higher age category. A retrospective observational study was conducted using match data collected over three seasons (2022–23 to 2024–25) from an elite youth soccer academy (n = 221). Three questions were examined: (i) whether promoted players differed from their regular teammates when competing in their original age category; (ii) whether they differed from the regular players of the higher age category when competing alongside them; and (iii) whether the same promoted players changed their physical outputs between the two age categories. External load variables included relative total distance, high-speed running, sprint distance, high intensity accelerations and decelerations. In their original age category, promoted players did not consistently differ from their regular teammates, although promoted Under-19 midfielders covered greater high-speed running distance. In the higher age category, promoted players generally showed physical outputs similar to those of the regular players of that category, although promoted Under-19 wingers covered greater sprint distance than regular Under-23 wingers. Within-player comparisons, often based on very few players, revealed position- and category-specific changes, with significant effects for decelerations in Under-16 and Under-19 centre-backs, high-speed running and sprint distance in Under-17 full-backs and strikers, and total distance in Under-19 strikers. These findings suggest that promotion is not associated with a consistent change in match physical outputs, but rather with specific changes according to age category, playing position, and physical variable, supporting individualized approaches to player development.

title: Analysis of attacking and defensive playing styles in the Africa cup of nations under-17 and under-20 soccer tournaments
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: Identifying and quantifying the different playing styles used by African youth soccer teams is important for objectively describing tactical approaches and team behaviours. This study aimed to identify and analyse team-match playing-style profiles during the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) Under-17 (U17) and Under-20 (U20) soccer tournaments. The AFCON U17 sample included 68 team-match observations from 34 matches, and the AFCON U20 sample included 60 team-match observations from 30 matches. Data were obtained from the Wyscout platform. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, multiple factor analysis, Ward.D2 hierarchical clustering, and outcome-appropriate regression models with standard errors clustered by team and match. The pooled analysis identified four team-match profiles: (1) limited progression, (2) controlled possession and progression, (3) balanced counterattacking, and (4) direct high-transition duel. Pooled Clusters 2 and 3 had higher estimated goal rates than Clusters 1 and 4 after adjustment for multiple comparisons, and U20 teams had a lower estimated goal rate than U17 teams. No pairwise differences in winning odds between clusters remained significant after adjustment, and no robust association was identified between cluster membership and goals conceded. The findings, therefore, provide stronger evidence for an association with goals scored than with match outcome.

title: Talent or timing? Skeletal maturity, biological maturation, and the relative age effect in youth athletes: a cross-sectional study from a high-performance sporting environment
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Aim We characterised the skeletal maturity profile, relative age distribution, and sport-type differences in biological maturation within a cohort of selected youth athletes from a high-performance sport environment. Methods Thirty-seven youth athletes (20 male, 17 female; mean chronological age: 14.92 ± 1.81 years) from 21 clubs across 15 sports in Split, Croatia, were assessed during the 2024–2025 competitive season. Skeletal age (SA) was estimated using the validated BAUSport™ SonicBone ultrasound system and compared with chronological age (CA). Athletes were classified as early (SA-CA ≥ + 1.0 year), on-time, or late maturers. Sports were assigned a priori to physical/power-dominant or skill/technical-aesthetic categories. The Relative Age Effect (RAE) was examined via chi-square goodness-of-fit and pairwise odds ratios; the primary sport-type contrast used the Mann–Whitney U test with rank-biserial r as the effect size index. Results Mean SA exceeded CA by 0.77 ± 0.89 years across the cohort, with 29.7% classified as early maturers and only 2.7% as late maturers. A marginal, preliminary RAE was observed ( χ 2 (3) = 8.08, p = 0.044, Cramér's V = 0.27), driven by Q1 overrepresentation (43%) rather than Q4 underrepresentation (24%); only Q1 versus Q3 was nominally significant (OR=4.00, 95% CI [1.34, 11.96]), not surviving Holm correction. The sport-type contrast was large and significant: SA-CA was +1.14 ± 0.81 years in physical/power-dominant sports versus +0.16 ± 0.67 years in skill/technical-aesthetic sports (U = 274.0, p = 0.00043, r = −0.70; Hedges’ g = 1.26, 95% CI [0.55, 1.97]). title: Auditory deprivation impairs badminton players’ stroke and anticipatory performance: a field experimental study
abstract: Background Accurate anticipation and precise motor execution are critical to success in badminton, yet most previous research has focused on visual information, with limited evidence regarding the role of auditory information. The present study used a two-part field design to investigate the effects of auditory information on stroke performance and anticipatory performance in badminton. Methods Thirty skilled badminton players completed both parts of the study in a fixed sequence. Part A employed a within-subjects design to examine the effects of modality type (audiovisual condition vs. visual-only condition) on reaction time and hitting accuracy in a smash-return task under the predictable-shot context (shot depth and direction known in advance). Part B employed the same participants and experimental design, with the addition of eye-tracking technology, to examine the effects of modality type on reaction time, mean fixation duration, and saccade frequency under an anticipatory condition (shot depth and direction unknown). Results In Part A, auditory deprivation significantly reduced stroke scores ( p < 0.001) and increased failure rates ( p < 0.001), but did not affect reaction time ( p = 0.376). In Part B, auditory deprivation prolonged reaction time ( p < 0.001) and shortened mean fixation duration ( p = 0.009), while saccade frequency showed no significant difference ( p = 0.862). title: Explainable machine learning audit of attribute rating relationships in Football Manager 2023
abstract: Background Football Manager data contain simulated player attributes generated within a proprietary game environment. They can reveal relationships within the rating system but cannot establish real-world talent-identification validity. Objective To audit how baseline attributes predict an internal Football Manager 2023 (FM2023) rating threshold, compare four untuned models under repeated cross-validation, and examine model-specific attribute-contribution stability across categories and positions. Methods We analyzed 2,282 anonymized male player profiles aged 15–18 years. The outcome was an FM2023 overall score of at least 10. Logistic regression, random forest, radial support vector machine (SVM), and a single-hidden-layer neural network were evaluated with three repeats of stratified five-fold cross-validation. We report receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC), precision-recall AUC (PR-AUC; average precision), F1 score, sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and Brier score. Logistic-regression contributions were calculated on the logit scale; position-specific top-five stability was evaluated with 1,000 bootstrap samples per modeled position. Results Logistic regression had the highest mean ROC-AUC (0.779 ± 0.033) and PR-AUC (0.380 ± 0.047), whereas the neural network had the highest mean F1 score (0.284 ± 0.055). At the prespecified 0.50 threshold, logistic-regression sensitivity was 0.132 and specificity was 0.983. Technical, physical, and mental attributes appeared among the ten highest-ranked contributions. title: Defensive synergies in association football: A systematic scoping review
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: The evolution of performance analysis in association football, supported by positional tracking, has improved understanding of collective behaviour. However, matches, and the defensive phase, are often summarised through statistics or outcomes. These indicators are poorly sensitive to the emergent organisation of out-of-possession play. From an ecological dynamics perspective, defensive coordination consists of functional couplings between defenders that create synergies reorganising according to task constraints. This scoping review mapped evidence on intra-team defensive synergies in association football following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR, including studies published between 01/01/2000 and 01/09/2025 (English/Italian/Spanish/Portuguese/French) that operationalised intra-team defensive coordination and synergies (≥2 defenders). Searches in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, and APA PsycInfo yielded 1217 records; after removing 363 duplicates, 854 records underwent screening and 131 full texts were assessed, resulting in 63 included studies. Common data sources were optical tracking and GPS/GNSS, combined with video/event data. Explicit defensive outcomes were reported in 21/63 studies. Contextual constraints were considered in most studies. The literature is growing, but remains heterogeneous and links between collective properties and defensive outcomes are not systematic. Minimum reporting standards, a core set of metrics, and stronger alignment between coordination measures and process-based outcomes consistent with the out-of-possession phase are needed.

title: Dimensionality reduction of space-related metrics in elite football using factor analysis
abstract: Spatial organisation is fundamental to understanding football tactics and phase-dependent coordination. However, the high intercorrelation between existing spatial metrics suggests significant redundancy. This study aims to identify the latent dimensions of spatial positioning in- and out-of-possession to refine the theoretical framework of space in professional football. An open-source dataset comprising seven male German Bundesliga matches was utilised to analyse team length, width, height, surface area, convex hull, team centroid, team spread, stretch index, Delaunay triangulation and Voronoi diagram. Ball possession status served as the independent variable. Spearman's rank correlation coefficients were calculated, while data suitability was examined using the KMO statistic and Bartlett's test of sphericity. An exploratory factor analysis was performed to identify underlying latent constructs. High intercorrelation among spatial metrics justified factor analysis to reduce redundancy. The analysis reveals three consistent spatial dimensions that explain team organisation, regardless of possession status. These dimensions account for 77.1% and 75.5% of the variance, respectively, with the first dimension representing almost half of the variance in each case. Factor analysis reduces complex spatial data into three functional dimensions: 'team dispersion', 'longitudinal dispersion', and 'longitudinal positioning'. This facilitates a concise yet comprehensive interpretation of tactical structures and performance analysis.

title: Physical fitness changes following group-based interval small-sided games among middle school soccer players
venue: Interpersona An International Journal on Personal Relationships
abstract: Objective: This study examined changes in aerobic fitness, resting and exercise heart rates, and sprint performance following an eight-week interval-based small-sided games program among middle school students participating in extracurricular soccer. Methods: Twenty-four male students from SMP Negeri 6 Palu, Indonesia, participated in a one-group pretest–posttest study involving 24 training sessions. The intervention consisted of 4 vs. 4 small-sided games played on a 30 × 25 m pitch in four 4-min bouts, separated by 2 min of passive recovery. Aerobic fitness was assessed using the Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 and expressed as estimated maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max). Heart rate was measured at rest and during exercise, while sprint performance was evaluated using a 30-m sprint test. Pretest and posttest measurements were compared using paired-samples t-tests. Results: Significant pre–post improvements were observed in estimated VO₂max, which increased from 49.82 ± 2.91 to 54.73 ± 3.08 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Resting heart rate decreased from 72.13 ± 4.87 to 67.08 ± 4.12 beats·min⁻¹, while exercise heart rate decreased from 181.46 ± 6.35 to 174.21 ± 5.92 beats·min⁻¹. The 30-m sprint time also improved from 4.82 ± 0.31 to 4.56 ± 0.28 s. All observed differences were statistically significant (p < .001). Conclusion: A systematically structured interval-based small-sided games program was associated with improvements in aerobic fitness, heart-rate responses, and sprint performance among middle school soccer players. This approach may provide a practical and engaging conditioning strategy for school-based extracurricular soccer programs. title: Effects of contextual factors on the external workload of top-up training sessions in an elite football team
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: This study aimed to analyse how match location and match outcome affect the external load of top-up sessions in professional football. Forty elite male players from a Spanish first-division team were monitored across 31 top-up sessions during the 2023/2024 competitive season, yielding 628 player-session observations for match-location analyses and 369 player-session observations for match-outcome analyses after excluding drawn matches. External load metrics were obtained via GPS, including total distance, high-speed running (HSR), sprint distance, and the number of accelerations and decelerations. Separate linear mixed-effects models tested location (home/away) and outcome (win/loss), with player as a random effect. Away matches produced longer session duration (F (1, 332) = 15.4, p < .001) with no other differences. Following a loss, sessions showed longer duration (F (1, 197) = 31.4, p < .001), total distance (F (1, 173) = 4.5, p = .036), sprint distance (F (1, 179) = 10.6, p = .001), accelerations >3 m/s 2 (F (1, 174) = 19.4, p < .001), and decelerations >3 m/s 2 (F (1, 170) = 12.5, p < .001), with no differences in high-speed running distance. Marginal R 2 values were low, while conditional R 2 values were higher, reflecting substantial between-player variability. Top-up demands were consistently higher after losses, suggesting that these sessions may be sensitive to competitive context rather than reflecting a stable match replication stimulus. More standardised loading targets may support more consistent weekly load management in underplayed players.

title: “You sink or swim”: An investigation into the experiences of applied performance analysts working in women's football
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: Performance analysis research within football has focussed on the outputs of systematic observation, quantification and analysis of performance; less attention has been given to the applied practices of performance analysts. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the experiences of applied performance analysts working within women's football, providing further insight beyond previous initial explorations. Ten performance analysts working with senior women's football teams (international n = 3; top-tier domestic n = 2; second-tier domestic n = 5) in the United Kingdom, participated in semi-structured interviews, which were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Two key themes were developed. Firstly, developing as an applied performance analyst in women's football, with four sub-themes of 1) alignment of learning opportunities to real-world practice, 2) preferences for learning opportunities, 3) navigating internal constraints and 4) navigating external constraints. Secondly, working as an applied performance analyst within women's football, with three sub-themes; 1) prioritisation of performance analysis provision, 2) implementing appropriate performance analysis provision and 3) challenges of working within women's football. The results demonstrate the breadth, depth and complexities of challenges and considerations in becoming, being and developing as an applied performance analyst within women's football. As such, the findings have wide-ranging implications for higher education institutions, academics, and development and learning professionals within football organisations and governing bodies, informing the development of aspiring and current analysts. title: Neuromuscular performance, physiological recovery, and maturation-referenced reference values in youth athletes: A cross-sectional study
abstract: This cross-sectional study characterized neuromuscular performance and acute physiological responses across age, sex, and biological maturation in 140 youth athletes (74 boys, 66 girls; 10–16 years), and described maturation-stratified distributions of two field measures. Participants completed 30-m sprint, countermovement jump (CMJ), standing long jump (SLJ), and handgrip testing; post-sprint heart-rate recovery (HRrec-30s) and a testing-battery perceived-exertion index (PEI) served as co-primary physiological/perceptual outcomes; maturity offset (Mirwald method) classified Pre-, Circa-, and Post-PHV subgroups; allometric scaling was used to account for body size; and a Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied across a pre-specified family of 58 pairwise comparisons and correlations (Tables 2–6). Boys outperformed girls across all neuromuscular tests (d = 0.63–0.76), whereas HRrec-30s and the perceived-exertion index did not differ significantly by sex. HRrec-30s was more strongly associated with maturity offset than with chronological age (r = 0.52 vs 0.46; η²p for maturation vs age groups 0.43 vs 0.39). Mean HRrec-30s was 27.8 ± 6.2 bpm in the Pre-PHV group and 45.3 ± 8.8 bpm in the Post-PHV group (p < 0.001, FDR-corrected). The perceived-exertion index was lower in more mature groups (7.5 ± 1.2 vs 6.3 ± 1.1). Sex and maturation differences in jump and strength performance remained after allometric scaling, although they were smaller. Maturation-stratified distributions reported here are preliminary and descriptive and are not decision thresholds; prospective, criterion-validated research is needed before they can be recommended for individual athlete monitoring or training-load decision-making.

title: Generational change in Slovenian youth sport participation
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Background Organised sport participation during adolescence provides important physical, psychosocial, and developmental benefits, yet long-term secular trends remain insufficiently understood. This study examined decade-long changes in organised sport participation among Slovenian adolescents using nationally representative repeated cross-sectional data from the Analysis of Children's Development in Slovenia (ACDSi). Methods Data included 5,027 adolescents aged 11–18 years assessed in 2013–2014 and 2023–2024. Organised sport participation, participation history, weekly training volume, sport-category distribution, and physical fitness were analysed overall and by sex and ISCED level. Between-wave differences were tested using Pearson's chi-square tests, and training volume and fitness outcomes using general linear models. Results Organised sport participation increased from 50.4% to 63.4% ( P < .001; OR = 1.71, 95% CI 1.52–1.91), with increases observed in both sexes and both ISCED levels. In the complete-case analysis, previous participation followed by discontinuation was more common in 2023–2024 than in 2013–2014 (27.1% vs. 19.7%), although participation-history data were incomplete for a substantial proportion of 2013–2014 non-participants. Among current participants, adjusted weekly training volume increased from 4.26 to 4.99 h/week in ISCED 2 and from 4.71 to 5.30 h/week in ISCED 3. Sport-category distribution changed modestly across the decade, particularly among girls, while team sports remained the dominant category. Physical fitness differed slightly across sport categories, with the clearest differences observed for standing long-jump and 60-m sprint performance. title: From sport-specific testing to competitive behavior in combat sports: matching designs to inferential questions
abstract: Sport-specific tests have improved the assessment of physical capacities in combat sports, but technical resemblance does not establish how a capacity is used against an opponent. This Perspective clarifies the evidence required to connect standardized measurement with predefined behavior under opposition. It distinguishes four related inferential questions concerning measurement, competitive association, contribution to competitive behavior, and transfer. The third question asks whether, and under which constraints, a measured capacity helps produce or regulate a predefined behavior during interaction with an opponent. These questions require different evidence without forming compulsory sequential stages or a uniform hierarchy of causal attribution. Drawing on measurement theory, representative design, and ecological dynamics, the argument follows kicking speed in taekwondo and grip strength in judo, supported by examples from other combat disciplines. It distinguishes integrated task performance from isolated capacities, capacity magnitude from individual use, and behavior from effectiveness and competitive success. Constrained opponent tasks can test whether capacity–behavior relationships vary with theoretically relevant constraints, but such interactions do not independently identify causal mechanisms. Longitudinal changes may be consistent with transfer while remaining compatible with familiarization, technical learning, or other intervention components. Standardized tests, opponent tasks, simulated bouts, and competition may therefore provide complementary evidence when the construct, behavioral criterion, opposition, and permissible inference are specified prospectively. title: Playing Surface Characteristics and Their Effects on Football Performance Across Multiple Surface Types: A Systematic Review
abstract: The characteristics of the playing surface are increasingly recognized as key determinants of football-specific performance. This systematic review synthesizes mechanistic and applied evidence on how natural grass, artificial turf, and sand influence physical, physiological, neuromuscular, and perceptual outcomes in football players. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science was conducted from database inception to 17 June 2026. Eligible studies included original peer-reviewed research involving football players performing football-related activities on natural grass, artificial turf, or other playing surfaces, provided that natural grass or artificial turf was included as a comparison condition. Risk of bias was assessed using the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized intervention studies and the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale adapted for cross-sectional studies (NOS-xs). Results were synthesized using a qualitative narrative approach because of substantial methodological heterogeneity across study designs, surface comparisons, and outcome measures. A total of 814 records were identified, of which 16 studies met the eligibility criteria. Locomotor responses were the most surface-sensitive domain: several studies reported greater external running demands on artificial turf, including higher sprint frequency, acceleration demands, and total running distance; however, results were heterogeneous and some studies observed no meaningful differences between surfaces. Sand consistently imposed greater metabolic cost and reduced running efficiency. title: The play that never happened: validating a counterfactual football simulator without ground truth
authors: José María García de Marina López
abstract: Section: Preprints Categories: Sport Science Keywords: football, tracking data, counterfactual simulation, model validation, pre-registration, decision models, multi-agent trajectories Counterfactual questions are the ones coaches ask most, and the hardest to validate: the alternative play never happened, so there is nothing to score it against. We present PlayLab, an interactive simulator that takes any real moment of a football match from broadcast tracking data, lets the user change it, and plays the next 20 s forward in a browser at 10 Hz. It is assembled from small, separately fitted components (defensive and attacking movement, pressing, goalkeeping, pass flight and completion, option listing, two decision policies, shooting and ball loss), fitted on the Saudi Pro League with SkillCorner tracking. We propose a three-layer validation protocol for simulators without counterfactual ground truth: component replay on held-out matches, stepped as the simulator steps them; decision-outcome evaluation on 59,972 real passes; and distributional plausibility of free-running chains on banks of real starting moments, with every change accepted or rejected by pre-registered pass marks. abstract: This dataset contains anonymized participant-level data from a randomized study examining the effects of a physical literacy-based preparation program and subsequent linear and nonlinear pedagogical approaches on football shooting skill acquisition in children aged 8–9 years. title: TOMADA DE DECISÃO E APRENDIZAGEM TÁTICA NO FUTEBOL ESCOLAR: EVIDÊNCIAS A PARTIR DE ABORDAGENS BASEADAS EM JOGOS
abstract: O ensino de futebol na Educação Física escolar demanda experiências que integrem execução motora, leitura de jogo, cooperação e tomada de decisão. Este artigo analisa criticamente evidências sobre abordagens baseadas em jogos e seu potencial para desenvolver aprendizagem tática em turmas escolares heterogêneas. Realizou-se revisão sistematizada qualitativa com síntese narrativa de literatura científica e documentos curriculares, sem coleta de dados primários ou metanálise própria. Foram examinados os fundamentos do Teaching Games for Understanding, propostas táticas centradas no jogo, princípios da pedagogia não linear, jogos reduzidos, mediação docente e instrumentos de avaliação contextualizada. Revisões recentes indicam efeitos promissores sobre determinadas medidas de tomada de decisão, mas apontam heterogeneidade dos procedimentos, dos desfechos e da qualidade metodológica dos estudos. A análise evidencia que o jogo modificado não garante aprendizagem quando faltam objetivos claros, distribuição de oportunidades e acompanhamento das decisões. Discute-se a necessidade de articular técnica e tática, reconhecer comportamentos sem posse, assegurar participação inclusiva e diferenciar medidas de desempenho de evidências de aprendizagem duradoura. Conclui-se que abordagens baseadas em jogos oferecem recursos pedagógicos relevantes, desde que implementadas com planejamento, reflexão, avaliação criteriosa e atenção às condições da escola.
summary: Revisión narrativa que valora los enfoques basados en juegos (TGfU, pedagogía no lineal, juegos reducidos) para el fútbol escolar. Concluye que son prometedores para la decisión táctica, pero la evidencia es heterogénea y depende de la planificación, la mediación y la evaluación.

Síntesis por unidades temáticas, apoyada sobre todo en las revisiones de González-Valero (2024), Manninen (2025) y Breed (2025).
results: Las revisiones recientes muestran efectos prometedores en medidas de decisión, pero variables según el resultado: los beneficios en decisión no siempre van acompañados de mejoras en conocimiento o ejecución motora. Un juego modificado no garantiza aprendizaje sin objetivos claros, reparto de oportunidades y seguimiento de las decisiones.
conclusions: Los enfoques basados en juegos son un recurso pedagógico relevante si se planifican, se acompañan con mediación docente y se evalúan con criterio, sin oponerlos al trabajo técnico.
limitations: Búsqueda no exhaustiva, sin protocolo, sin doble cribado ni extracción estandarizada; sin datos primarios.

title: Perceptual-cognitive skills in talent development environments: Coaches' perspectives and practices
abstract: Despite the recognised importance of perceptual-cognitive skills (PCS) for future professional football performance, there remains limited applied research examining how practitioners engage in this area of player development. The aim of this thesis was to critically examine how PCS are identified and assessed within talent development environments in football. Recognising the critical role of PCS in talent identification (TI) and talent development (TD), this research adopted an applied perspective to evaluate current practices and identify pathways for enhancing these processes. A central objective was to bridge the gap between academic insights and practical applications, providing actionable recommendations for industry practitioners. Chapter 2 presents a scoping review of the existing literature on PCS in football, examining their support within TD contexts and identifying gaps in the research. Building on this foundation, Chapter 4 investigates academy coaches’ perceptions and approaches to identifying and assessing PCS, alongside associated challenges and the current state of educational provision in this domain. Chapter 5 extends the scope of these findings by examining the generalisability of these findings through a national survey. The findings from these chapters informed the design of Chapter 6, which explores the co-creation of a shared mental model within a football academy in the UK. This intervention aimed to improve alignment and standardisation in the identification and assessment of PCS, offering insights into its feasibility and potential impact. The findings of this thesis contribute to the evolving understanding of PCS in football, addressing practical and knowledge gaps. The work provides actionable recommendations for enhancing coaching practice

title: Strokes towards more evidence-based swimming lessons: motor learning and motivation in children
abstract: Swimming skills are essential for safety, recreation, and health. However, basic swimming skills are not always retained or transferred to real-world aquatic settings after initial acquisition. In addition, individuals may lack the motivation to continue swimming and maintain their skills. Identifying effective motor learning methods that promote skill acquisition, retention, transfer, and sustained motivation is therefore important for strengthening evidence-based swimming lessons. The aim of this thesis was to help make swimming lessons more evidence-based by examining how children can learn swimming skills effectively and remain motivated to swim. It focused on several theoretically grounded motor learning methods: explicit verbal instruction, video modeling, analogy learning, external-focus-of-attention learning, and the constraints-led approach (CLA). It also considered motivation from the perspective of self-determination theory (SDT), which emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as key drivers for intrinsic motivation. Chapter 2 examined current practices in Dutch swimming lessons designed to motivate children. To this end, 128 lessons taught by various instructors were observed. Instructors generally supported children’s need for relatedness, but often thwarted autonomy and offered limited competence support. Lessons based on SDT principles scored higher on all three needs, with a significant difference for autonomy. The teaching program was the only significant predictor of instructors’ use of SDT principles. These findings suggest that integrating SDT principles into teaching programs may improve the support of children’s psychological needs, particularly autonomy. title: Physical performance indicators for talent identification in youth soccer: an umbrella review with an update of recent primary evidence
abstract: Sprint, change-of-direction (COD), jump and endurance tests are used in youth soccer selection, but differences between selected and non-selected players do not establish whether those tests predict later success. This review will synthesise systematic reviews of physical and physiological indicators associated with selection, competitive level and subsequent progression. A complementary systematic search will identify eligible primary evidence not represented in those reviews, including recent studies and earlier omissions. The two evidence streams will remain distinguishable throughout selection, appraisal and synthesis. Biological maturation, relative age and the selection context will be considered when interpreting findings.

title: Comparative effects of internal and external feedback during learning of a complex motor skill.
venue: The Journal of sports medicine and physical fitness
abstract: The influence of attentional focus on motor learning has been widely studied, yet evidence regarding how focus effects vary across learning stages and complex tasks remains inconclusive. The present study examined the impact of external vs. internal focus instructions on the acquisition and short-term retention of a complex manual skill task. Sixteen healthy novice adults (8 males and 8 females; mean age: 26.3±3.8 years), with no prior experience in twirling or organized sports participation, were randomly assigned to either an external focus (EFA) or an internal focus (IFA) instructional group. Following an initial familiarization phase, participants completed three acquisition blocks of 15 trials each (45 practice trials in total) and a 15-trial retention test performed the following day. Performance was evaluated in terms of movement effectiveness and technical execution quality. Participants receiving EFA instructions exhibited superior performance improvements during acquisition and higher retention scores than those receiving IFA instructions. Between-group comparisons revealed significant differences favoring the EFA group across all execution categories (all P<.05). These findings contribute to the understanding of how attentional focus manipulations influence motor behavior across learning stages, highlighting the potential utility of external focus strategies in complex motor tasks. Limitations related to sample size and instructional content are discussed, and implications for future research on attentional mechanisms in motor learning are considered.

title: EXAMINATION OF THE STRATEGY OF HUNGARIAN YOUTH FOOTBALL ORGANISATIONS
abstract: Youth education is of strategic importance for sport enterprises, as it contributes to long-term sustainability and competitiveness. A well-designed youth program supports the identification and development of talent, while the strategy adopted by sports organizations influences both athlete development and the long-term operation of the organization. The research examined the entire vertical of Hungarian youth football. A well-structured strategy supports the efficient allocation of resources, the professional and infrastructural development of athletes, and the integration of home-grown players into adult teams. It can also contribute to economic stability by reducing transfer costs, supporting diversified sources of income and increasing the attractiveness of organizations to sponsors and investors. The results highlighted that talent development, and training strategies differ between academies and lower-ranked organizations. The sample also revealed limited employee involvement in setting strategic goals, which may reduce employee engagement and the effectiveness of strategy implementation in practice.

title: The influence of differentiated instruction on students’ motivation in physical education
abstract: Background Physical education (PE) classes are intrinsically heterogeneous, yet students differing in competence, readiness, and motivation are often exposed to uniform instructional demands. Differentiated instruction has been widely advocated as a response to learner diversity, but rigorous evidence regarding its motivational consequences and underlying psychological processes remains limited. Methods We conducted a two-arm cluster-randomized longitudinal trial across 12 secondary schools in Zhengzhou, China. Forty-eight teacher–class clusters comprising 1,152 students aged 12–15 years were randomized to a 12-week differentiated-instruction intervention or usual PE. The intervention systematically adapted task challenge, instructional support, grouping, pacing, progression, and bounded choice to students’ readiness and learning needs. Assessments were completed at baseline (T0), during intervention (T1), post-intervention (T2), and follow-up (T3). The primary outcome was autonomous motivation at T2; secondary outcomes were psychological need satisfaction and frustration, controlled motivation, amotivation, and PE engagement. Three-level longitudinal mixed-effects models and multilevel longitudinal mediation models were used. title: Clustering professional football players using Gaussian mixture models: A case study of the English Premier League 2024/25
abstract: The increasing availability of detailed football performance data has created new opportunities for identifying player archetypes and informing recruitment and tactical decision-making. Most existing clustering approaches assign each player to a single group, despite the reality that many modern footballers perform hybrid roles spanning multiple stylistic categories. Performance data for 314 outfield players from the 2024/25 English Premier League season are analysed using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) applied to principal component representations of player statistics. Unlike hard-assignment methods such as k-means, the GMM provides probabilistic cluster memberships, allowing uncertainty and role hybridity to be quantified. Seven player archetypes are identified in the full dataset. Posterior membership probabilities reveal a subset of players whose profiles span multiple clusters, providing an objective measure of tactical flexibility and stylistic ambiguity. Further analyses within defender, midfielder, and forward groups recover position-specific sub-archetypes and highlight exceptional outliers. The results demonstrate that model-based clustering provides a flexible and interpretable framework for identifying latent structure in high-dimensional performance data while explicitly quantifying uncertainty in cluster membership. More broadly, the approach is readily transferable to other sports and domains in which individuals exhibit overlapping characteristics and cannot be adequately represented by hard cluster assignments alone.

title: Active Inference and Predictive Processing for Skill Learning: Implications for Skill Acquisition in Coaching Practice.
abstract: This paper explores the potential of the Active Inference Framework (AIF) and Predictive Processing (PP) to advance our understanding of skill and motor learning with a key focus on introducing these concepts to coaches and highlighting their practical implications. Conceptual frameworks such as Information Processing (IP) and Ecological Dynamics (ED) have contributed significantly to the field of skill acquisition. Despite recent efforts to reconcile these perspectives, however, their fundamentally different theoretical foundations concerning perception, cognition and learning processes pose substantial challenges for integration. Although ED has made valuable contributions through its focus on perception-action coupling and direct interaction with the environment, it involves adopting a radical ontological stance that emphasises rejecting traditional cognitive constructs that can complicate practical applications in coaching. Conversely, IP's reliance on concepts such as stored motor programs and the view of the brain as a computer-like processor can limit its ability to account for the dynamic, emergent nature of skill acquisition in real-world contexts. We suggest that AIF offers a parsimonious perspective, accommodating the dynamic, embodied and enactive nature of skill acquisition without the necessity of committing to either framework's specific assumptions. This perspective provides practitioners with a coherent and flexible framework for understanding and designing skill learning interventions, offering a practically useful account of skill acquisition for coaching practice.

title: Mismatches Between Talent Identification and Development Models: Why Their Distinct Natures Must Be Nurtured.
venue: Perspectives on psychological science : a journal of the Association for Psychological Science
abstract: The identification and development of talent are top priorities across education, sports, business, and the arts. A major challenge lies in developing and applying appropriate models in both science and practice. Talent-identification models should center around predicting future excellence, whereas talent-development models should focus on how skills, resources, and their interactions change over time on the path to excellence. After providing an overview of the literature on talent-identification and talent-development models, I will argue that these models are often misapplied across domains: Talent-identification models are frequently used for talent development, and vice versa, which hampers progress in both scientific research and practical application. To address this issue, I propose a dual-path approach to nurture the distinct natures of talent-identification and talent-development models. For talent development, longitudinal processes involving relevant variables (e.g., psychosocial, cognitive, and physical) should be studied and evaluated at the individual level. For talent identification, predictive models incorporating relevant variables need to be tested, and their optimal and consistent application in real-world settings should be evaluated. This dual-path approach offers opportunities to advance psychological science and practice in identifying and developing talent across diverse domains of achievement.
summary: Perspectiva de Den Hartigh que argumenta que los modelos de identificación del talento (predicción) y de desarrollo (proceso) tienen naturalezas distintas y no deben confundirse.

title: Visual Search Strategies and Decision-Making in Highly Trained Female Youth Basketball Players: A Quasi-Experimental in Situ Study of Gaze Behavior during Pick-and-Roll Plays
abstract: This study explored how U16 female basketball players direct their visual attention and make decisions during side pick-and-roll situations under realistic game conditions. Twelve experienced players participated in 4v4 scenarios, where defensive strategies were systematically varied to reflect authentic tactical challenges. Using Pupil Core eye-tracking glasses operating at 120 Hz, we recorded gaze behavior without restricting natural movement on the court. Gaze data were synchronized with nine predefined tactical areas of interest using the surface tracker plugin, enabling detailed analysis of visual search behavior in dynamic environments. Time-series, entropy, and gaze transition analyses revealed that offensive decisions were closely shaped by defensive constraints. “Pass to Roller” and “Pass to Corner” were the most frequent responses, depending on the defensive strategy in place. Players’ gaze patterns evolved throughout each trial, with final fixations on decision targets occurring mainly in the last phase of action preparation. Focused visual strategies were more common in shooting and passing decisions, whereas broader search behavior’s characterized driving actions. These findings show that young players adapt their visual attention on a moment-to-moment basis in response to tactical demands, and support the relevance of in situ eye-tracking as a tool for understanding perception and decision-making in youth basketball.

title: From talent labels to stable expertise.
abstract: Early achievement and subjective labeling can be a weak guide to sustained expertise. Yet talent labels shape access to coaching, practice, and competition, so selection alters the conditions under which early judgements are later evaluated. This Perspective article proposes a conceptual framework in which labeling, selection, development, transition, and stabilisation are recursively linked processes. Its outcome, stable expertise, is repeated superior, domain-specific performance over a prespecified period that includes substantive changes in performance demands. The central claim is that the same outcome may reflect restricted opportunity, limited learning, difficulty adapting to new demands, or difficulty maintaining an established standard. Distinguishing these explanations requires separate observations of judgements, opportunity allocation, capacity change, adaptation, and performance over time. Five falsifiable propositions, each paired with a prospective design, specify when early indicators should lose predictive value, how selection shapes capacity through allocated opportunities, which junior advantages are unlikely to persist, and how adaptation, regulation, and support sustain or restore expert performance. The evidence is drawn mainly from sport; other domains require their own measures and tests. For talent systems, the framework implies treating labels as provisional predictions, reassessed against the opportunities they have created.

title: Decision-Making in Basketball: The Interplay between Cognitive Processes and Motor Execution
abstract: This study aimed to explore the relationship between dribbling behavior preceding passing and shooting patterns, and its implications for the interplay between decision-making efficiency and motor execution across four competitive basketball levels: the National Basketball Association (NBA), the EuroLeague, and European national teams, and the under-16 (U16) and under-18 (U18) European national teams. A total of 32 games (eight from each level) were analyzed to identify performance variables associated with success. Actions involving zero dribbles and sequences of three or more dribbles (3+) emerged as the most effective offensive patterns, reflecting the complementarity between rapid, intuitive decisions and deliberate, well-planned actions. Moreover, at the higher competitive levels, assists were more frequently produced following zero-dribble situations, underscoring the efficiency of quick, collective ball movement among elite players. Professional players were more likely to draw fouls during extended dribbling sequences, suggesting greater technical adaptability compared to lower competitive level players. Overall, these findings emphasize the integration of decision-making and motor execution as hallmarks of basketball expertise, highlighting the importance of developing both intuitive and deliberate decision processes in training.

title: When the Clock Is Wrong
abstract: Section: Preprints Categories: Sport Science, Elite Athletics, Measurement Keywords: soccer, athlete tracking, Sports events, data quality, performance monitoring, synchronisation Practitioners increasingly link coded match events to positional data to quantify the physical demands of individual actions, yet event timestamps are not perfectly aligned with tracking data. This study quantified how this misalignment affects event-level external load flags. Three elite German football matches (3,561 events, 61 players) with frame-level, hand-annotated event times served as ground truth. Four timestamp conditions were compared: the raw provider feed, a best-case constant clock correction and two synchronisation algorithms ( ETSY and ELASTIC ). Speed and acceleration flags were derived for the acting player in a ±2 s window and evaluated on 3,186 common events. Raw timestamps were misaligned by a median of 0.76 s, with 39.2% of events misaligned by more than 1 s. Using raw timestamps, 18.5% (95% CI 13.9–23.8%) of sprint-linked and 27.9% (24.4–31.4%) of sustained-acceleration-linked events were missed, and each additional second of error increased the odds of a missed flag 2.6- to 4.9-fold. A constant clock correction gave no significant improvement because errors were event-specific, whereas ELASTIC reduced misses to 1.0–2.1% (all p < 0.001). Event-level physical metrics should therefore be computed only after validated synchronisation.

title: Comparison of automated and manual performance analysis tools in amateur padel: a descriptive case study
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Background Automated match-analysis systems increasingly provide technical-tactical reports in padel, but their agreement with manual observation remains unclear. The aim was to describe discrepancies between aggregate match statistics displayed by Padmi and manual observational coding in amateur padel. Methods Three amateur male matches involving one focal player were retrospectively analysed from video using the Padmi app (version 1.3). Six shot types (forehand, backhand, forehand volley, backhand volley, bandeja, smash) and three outcome categories were coded manually and compared with Padmi's aggregate reports. Signed and absolute differences were calculated for shot frequencies and percentage-point differences for outcomes. Shot-level agreement metrics were not calculated because raw Padmi event-level data were unavailable. Results Manual coding identified 891 shots, whereas Padmi displayed 757 (−15.0%). Padmi displayed fewer shots in all matches (−11.4% to −19.2%). Discrepancies varied by shot type: forehand −28.3%, backhand −20.0%, bandeja −3.5%, smash −44.8%, forehand volley +27.2%, backhand volley +5.9%. Overall outcome distributions were similar, but larger shot-specific discrepancies emerged for the smash, bandeja, and forehand volley. Conclusions Padmi's user-facing aggregate statistics differed from manual coding in this small case study. Automated reports may be useful for broad feedback but require cautious interpretation and further independent validation for detailed technical-tactical decisions.

title: Differences in the external and internal load according to the player’s position Diferencias en la carga externa e interna en función de la posición de juego Diferenças na carga externa e interna consoante a posição de jogo
abstract: Background/Objectives: the load analysis in football has consolidated as an essential factor for optimising performance and reducing the injury risk in players at different competitive levels. External and internal loads in football present significant changes according to the player position, and these differences must be considered in the training plan and periodization of the load during the season and in injury prevention. The study aimed to evaluate and compare external, internal, and neuromuscular load in senior football players in Portugal across different players’ positions. Methods: Wimu ProTM (Hudl, Nebraska, United States) and Garmin Heart Rate bands (Garmin International Inc., Kansas, USA) were used to quantify and evaluate the external and internal load of the players. A total of 121 athletes were assessed which were divided into 5 player positions. Results: significant differences were observed between players’ positions across several external and neuromuscular load variables (p >0.001). Considering the distance, midfields reported higher mean values (118.20±12.41) compared to the other positions. Considering the Player Load, significant differences were reported among the different positions (p <0.001; ε² = 0.285) and Total Impacts/min (p <0.001; ε² = 0.312). Regarding the internal load (heart rate), a significant difference was observed for the variable Avg. HR (bpm) (p = 0.024; ε² = 0.062) when comparing GK with all the other positions. In the same line, the GKs were those who reflected the lowest values according to the Avg. HR. Conclusions: the inclusion of kinematics, neuromuscular, and cardiac variables allows the coaching staff a higher comprehension of the sports performance and facilitates the decision-making of the performance manager.
